text.p: Thyssen Handelsunion AG said on Thursday its pretax profit plummeted to 1.2 million marks ($732,400) in the year ended September 30, but it expected to rebound sharply this year.

Pretax profit at the trade and services unit of Thyssen AG was 227 million marks in 1994/95, and the company aims to restore it to above 100 million marks in the current year, barring unforeseen extraordinary outlays, chairman Hans-Erich Forster told a news conference.

The year 1995/96 "was one of the most difficult years in our history" due to higher materials costs, difficult market conditions, sluggishness in the construction sector and start-up costs in telecommunications, Forster said.
On a net basis, the company posted a loss of 53 million marks, which was largely covered by a 47.7 million mark transfer from the parent company Thyssen AG, he said.

Group income from ordinary activities fell to 42.4 million marks from 227 million marks, but results were further hammered by extraordinary outlays of 41.2 million marks, mainly for restructuring its recyling business in east Germany, versus nil the year before.
Sales were 18.18 billion marks, down from 18.265 billion.
The unit is relying on stringent cost management and vigorous internationalisation to help it overcome lingering recessionary factors.

While the company feels it has a solid basis in its material business, which accounts for nearly 50 percent of revenue, it is restructuring its construction, logistics, recycling and telecommunications operations. It aims to boost materials sales to 15 billion marks by the year 2000.
Sales in the first quarter of the current business year were slightly less than in the year-earlier quarter.
Forster said the German economic slowdown of the past year came after the October-December 1995 period but was still a drag on sales in the same quarter of 1996.
Lower steel prices also hurt sales, but prices have begun to turn around since the start of 1997, company officials said.
Thyssen Handelsunion plans to trim investments to 800 million marks in the current business year, from 940 million marks last year.

It posted a loss of 178.3 million marks on its share of mobile phone subsidiary E-Plus Mobilfunk GmbH. Forster said the loss was within plan, given the start-up nature of the business, which entails outlays for capital infrastructure.

Subsidiary Thyssen Telecom AG also showed a loss of 66 million marks. Thyssen Handelsunion invested 357.1 million marks in Thyssen Telecom in the year ended September 30, over one-third of its total group investment.
Comparison figures were not immediately available.

Thyssen Telecom, which had been a leading contender for an alliance with DBKom, the telecommunications arm of national railway Deutsche Bahn AG, last year lost that bid to its competitor Mannesmann Mobilfunk GmbH.

Following the DBKom debacle, Thyssen is concentrating its telecommunications activities on those areas of the business it can handle alone, without an alliance with a strong, permanent partner, Forster said.
Thyssen's telecommunications strategy will rest on mobile phone units E-Plus and DFR, its fixed network PlusNet, and multimedia services for other network operators, Forster said.
The workforce shrank to 31,791 last fiscal year, down 133 from the year before, but actual job cuts were 1,700, partly offset by acquisitions and new hirings, company officials said.
